## In this lab: one sheet, three readers {#plan}

{{< include _plan-lab2-one-case-three-outputs.md >}}

[Make one output, **check three facts**, then make the next. Never all three at once.]{.big}

::: notes
**Before the clock starts.** Lab Two is one case, three readers. Part 1, twenty minutes: build one sheet from a case card and check it, then make a chart note, a patient handout and three slides from it, one at a time, checking three facts after each. Part 2, ten minutes: the same source in two tools, looking for one thing. Part 3, five minutes: a share-out where we apply the three-question check together. We do every step together: I run it on this screen, you run it on yours.
:::

## Three tabs, and nothing else {#setup}

::: {.lane}
[Tab 1: the call]{.node .same .grow} [+]{.op} [Tab 2: these slides]{.node .grow} [+]{.op} [Tab 3: your assistant, signed in]{.node .teal .grow}
:::

[▲ Every prompt has a Copy prompt button on its slide. I paste it in the chat too.]{.pointer}

- Part 2 adds a one more tab for your second option, for ten minutes.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## The privacy line
No patient identifiers into a consumer AI tool. Ever. Full stop. Case cards only.
:::

::: notes
**Before the clock starts.** Three tabs: the call, these slides (the link is in the chat), and the assistant, signed in. Every prompt and the case has a Copy prompt button on its slide, and I paste it in the chat too. Part 2 adds a one more tab for the second option from Lab One, for ten minutes. Case A is the default because its card is written for exactly these three outputs; anyone who wants another card says so in the chat and I paste it. Anyone without a tool yet follows your shared screen for the sheet and one output. The privacy line applies to every prompt you paste.

**Do.** Chat, thirty seconds: everyone types "ready" when the three tabs are open. Start part 1 when most have typed it.
:::

# Part 1: One sheet, three outputs [20 min]{.time} {#part-1}

::: notes
**Goal.** Everyone leaves part 1 with a sheet they checked, and a chart note, a patient handout and a three-slide teaching version, each checked on three facts before the next was made.

**Have ready.** Your own assistant open in a window you can share, to run each step as the group does. Case A, and your own full run of part 1, so you know what a mismatch looks like. A saved backup set to share on screen if a tool goes down.

**Clock.** 0:00 the picture. 0:30 the sheet. 4:00 chart note: make, then check. 9:00 handout: make, then check. 14:00 slides: make, then check. 19:00 what your table found, in the chat. 20:00 time.

**Watch for.** Skipping the sheet check to reach the outputs faster: the commonest failure. Making all three outputs and checking none: stop them after each one. Judging by fluency: "this one reads better". A table full of ticks that nobody looked at.

**If asked.** Why a new chat for each output? An error in one cannot leak into the next, and each draws on the sheet, not on the others. Can I use my own case? A card is safer; if you do, apply the privacy checklist first.

**Bridge.** "Same comparison as Day One, new task: look at what the tool added, not which answer sounded better."
:::

## Step 1: build the sheet, then fix it {#p1-sheet}

::: {.paste-long}
{{< include _paste-source-of-truth-sheet.md >}}

[▲ Copy prompt on your slide, with Case A under it. Paste both into a new chat. Then check the sheet against the card: **invented, omitted, altered**.]{.pointer}

::: {.move .solo}
[Solo · 3 min 30 sec]{.tag} Build the sheet, check it, fix it by hand.
:::

::: notes
**3:30.** Build the sheet and fix it yourself before anything else. No patient identifiers into a consumer AI tool. Ever. Full stop. Cards only. Then check the sheet against the card line by line for invented, omitted, altered. This step decides everything after it: an error left in the sheet is copied into all three outputs. It is the verification workflow one level up, with the card as the source.

**Do.** Tell them to click Copy prompt on their slide, and paste the block into the chat too, then paste Case A under it. Run it on your screen as they run it on theirs. Near minute 3, ask everyone to type "sheet checked" as they finish; do not move on while many are still reading. At 4:00 say: new chat for each output.
:::

## Check the chart note {#p1-note-check}

::: {.card .teal}
[Against the sheet, tick each one]{.t}

[]{.chk} Losartan 50 mg once daily, with amlodipine 5 mg

[]{.chk} Creatinine and potassium in 2 weeks

[]{.chk} Review in 4 weeks
:::

[Tick it if it matches. If not, write **altered** or **omitted**.]{.pointer}

::: {.move .solo}
[Solo · 2 min 30 sec]{.tag} Check the three facts.
:::

::: notes
**2:30.** Stop and check three facts against the sheet: the medicines and doses, the repeat blood tests and when, and the review. Tick the box if the note says exactly what the sheet says. If not, write one word: altered, or omitted. If two disagree, go to the sheet and the card, not to whichever output reads better. Then ask whether the sheet itself was the source of the error.

**Do.** Tick your own on the shared screen as they tick theirs. Say "new chat" at 9:00 on the part clock, and "second output next" at 8:30. Watch the chat for stuck tools; share your saved backup set for anyone without a working tool.
:::

## Check the handout {#p1-handout-check}

::: {.card .teal}
[Against the sheet, tick each one]{.t}

[]{.chk} Losartan 50 mg once daily, with amlodipine 5 mg

[]{.chk} Creatinine and potassium in 2 weeks

[]{.chk} Review in 4 weeks

[]{.chk} Nothing the sheet does not say
:::

[Friendly advice, warnings and reassurance are the usual extras. Case A names no warning signs.]{.pointer}

::: {.move .solo}
[Solo · 2 min 30 sec]{.tag} Check the three facts, then read it once more.
:::

::: notes
**2:30.** The same three facts. A fact left out on purpose gets a dash. Then read the handout once more for anything the sheet does not say: friendly advice, warnings, reassurance. Extra content is easiest to miss here. Case A names no warning signs to return for, so a handout that lists some did not get them from the card: delete the list, or write your own.

**Do.** Tick your own on the shared screen. Watch the chat for the first "it added a warning list"; thank them. Say "new chat" at 14:00 on the part clock.
:::

## What good looks like {#p1-good}

| The fact | Chart note | Handout | Slides |
|--------------------------------------|:-------:|:-------:|:-------:|
| Losartan 50 mg once daily, with amlodipine 5 mg | []{.chk} | []{.chk} | []{.chk} |
| Creatinine and potassium in 2 weeks | []{.chk} | []{.chk} | []{.chk} |
| Review in 4 weeks | []{.chk} | []{.chk} | []{.chk} |

Every box has a tick, a word or a dash. A table with no mismatch is a good result if you checked.

::: {.move .chat}
[Chat · 1 min]{.tag} Type what your table found: all matched, one differed, or extra content.
:::

::: notes
**1:00.** Check yourself against this: the sheet fixed before any output existed; each output checked before the next was made; every box with a tick, a word or a dash. A table with no mismatch is a good result if you checked; a table nobody filled in is not.

**Do.** Chat, one minute: type what your table found. Pick three volunteers for part 3 from the answers: one mismatch, one whose handout added content, one clean. Ask each by name in the chat to be ready to share. Leave them with the line: one sheet, three outputs, three facts; an output that disagrees with the sheet is wrong, however fluent it sounds.
:::

# Part 2: Same source, two tools [10 min]{.time} {#part-2}

::: notes
**Goal.** Everyone repeats Day One's comparison on a Day Two task and says what held and what did not, from what they could see.

**Have ready.** Your two tool windows from Day One open for the shared screen. A saved run to share on screen if a tool goes down.

**Clock.** 0:00 read the source. 1:00 paste the prompt and the source into both tools. 4:00 read each against the source, two rows. 8:00 the two closing lines. 10:00 time.

**Watch for.** Part 2 turning into a brand debate: point at the table. Judging by fluency: "this one reads better". A tool that will not take the pasted text, or answers from its own sources: they write it down; that is a result, not a failure.

**If asked.** Which tool won? That is not the result: the two rows in the table are. A second option that cannot take pasted text, as a plain literature search cannot: ask both for the evidence behind one number in the source, such as the 135/85 threshold, and compare what each lets you check.

**Bridge.** "Last five minutes: do together what you have been doing alone. Pick the one output you would least want to be wrong."
:::

:::

## Look for one thing {#p2-look}

[Did it add anything the source does not say?]{.big}

| | General assistant | Second option |
|---------------------------------------------|-------------------|-------------------|
| Added something the source does not say? | yes / no | yes / no |
| Every number copied exactly? | yes / no | yes / no |

If a tool cited something, open it before you believe it.

::: {.move .solo}
[Solo · 4 min]{.tag} Read each summary against the source and fill in the two rows.
:::

::: notes
**4:00.** Read each summary against the source. Two rows only. Did it add anything that the source does not say? A finding, a threshold, a caveat, a number. And did it copy every number exactly as the source wrote it? If a tool cited something, open it before you believe it. Compare what you can see, not which answer sounded better.

**Do.** Read your own two summaries on the shared screen and answer the two rows aloud. At minute 3 of the part, say: one minute left on the table. If the group drifts into which tool is better, point at the two rows.
:::

:::

...because of something you saw.
:::
:::

::: {.move .solo}
[Solo · 2 min]{.tag} Finish the two lines.
:::

::: notes
**2:00.** Finish the two lines: did the Day One pattern hold, and which tool you would use for this job, and why. Good looks like this. You compared on things you can see. If a tool cited something, you opened it. Your because names something you observed, not a feeling about the tool. You can close the one more tab now.

**Do.** Say your own two lines aloud. Read out two "because" lines from the chat if people post them. Leave them with the line: same task, two ways of answering; look at what each added. Which one sounded better is not a result.
:::

# Part 3: Share-out [5 min]{.time} {#part-3}

::: notes
**Goal.** Everyone applies the three-question check to an output someone else made: the move they will need when a colleague hands them an AI-drafted note and asks if it looks fine.

**Have ready.** Your three volunteers from part 1: one with a mismatch, one whose handout added content, one clean. A saved backup output to share if nobody can. The three questions are on the slides.

**Clock.** 0:00 everyone picks the output they would least want to be wrong. 1:00 two or three volunteers share. 4:00 everyone writes one thing to change. 5:00 time.

**Watch for.** "It looked fine" instead of a named fact and where it was checked. A "no" with no next step. The group questioning the person, not the output. Losing this part: protect these five minutes and shorten part 2 instead.

**If asked.** What if my answer to a question is no? That is a good answer here. What matters is what you do next: check the source, or delete the line.

**Bridge.** "Tomorrow is Day Three: what goes wrong, and what never goes in. Have ready the Lab One output you saved, which Lab Three uses, and one output from today, which the session Back to the rule uses."
:::

## Pick one output {#p3-pick}

[The one you would least want to be wrong.]{.big}

The patient handout is a good candidate: a patient will act on it. Put it beside its sheet.

::: {.move .solo}
[Solo · 1 min]{.tag} Choose it and put it beside its sheet. Volunteers: have your screen ready to share.
:::

::: notes
**1:00.** The last five minutes are for doing together what you have been doing alone: applying the check to something a colleague made. It is the same move you will need at work, when someone hands you an AI-drafted note and asks whether it looks fine. Pick the one output you would least want to be wrong. The patient handout is a good candidate, because a patient will act on it.

**Do.** Solo for a minute. Ask your three volunteers, by name in the chat, to have their screen ready. If one is missing, take another from the chat answers in part 1.
:::

1. Could I defend this to a colleague?
2. Does it point to something I can verify?

:::

::: notes
**3:00.** Each volunteer shares a screen with the output beside its sheet, reads two lines aloud, and names one fact they checked and where. Everyone answers the three questions in the chat for that output: could I defend this to a colleague, does it point to something I can verify, would I catch it if it were wrong. Read out two or three answers. A no is a good answer here: what matters is what the volunteer does next.

**Do.** Share, one volunteer at a time, about a minute each. The chat carries the three questions; no pair step is needed. If nobody can share, share your saved backup output and run the questions on it.
:::

## Part 3: what good looks like {#p3-good}

If the answer to any of these is no, that's the signal to slow down, not the finding to accept.

- The volunteer names a specific fact and where they checked it.
- A "no" comes with a next step.

::: {.move .solo}
[Solo · 1 min]{.tag} Write one thing you will change next time, in the sheet or in the prompt.
:::

::: notes
**1:00.** What good looks like: the volunteer names a specific fact and where they checked it, not "it looked fine". A no comes with a next step: check the source, or delete the line. Everyone questions the output, not the person. Then each person writes one thing to change next time, in the sheet or in the prompt. If time allows, ask which output you would send without one more read; the rule expects none.

**Do.** Solo for the last minute. Read out two or three changes if people post them in the chat. Leave them with the line: fluent is not verified; say what you checked, against what, and what you would still check. Then the bridge from the topic slide: Day Three tomorrow, and what to have ready.
:::

## If it goes wrong {#fixes}

| Problem | Fix |
|----------|---------------------|
| A real case turns up | Stop and use a card. Already pasted something? Follow the privacy checklist. |
| Tool slow, or quota gone | Switch to your other tool, or follow my shared backup set. Never use anyone else's login. |
| The sheet is prose, or longer than the card | Facts only, one per line. |
| The handout lists warning signs | Case A names none. Delete the list, or write your own. |
| Two outputs disagree | The sheet and the card decide. Fix the sheet, then rerun that output in a new chat. |
| A tool will not take your text | Write it down. That is a result, not a failure. |
| Missed what was pasted | Ask in the chat. I paste it again. |

::: notes
**On demand, no clock.** Keep this slide for when something goes wrong; do not present it. Answer in the chat with the row that fits. A real case is the one to stop for: say it without blame, send them to a card, and point to the privacy checklist for what to do next; Day Three covers why. A slow tool is not a failure of the lab: the sheet and two outputs are enough, then follow your backup set on screen.

**Do.** Chat the fix; do not read the table aloud. If the problem is a participant's call setup, the troubleshooting page covers it.
:::
